captions.instagram:
How does a telephone work?

Your voice squeezes a pinch of carbon, a current copies the sound, and a switch that steps once per pulse finds the other phone. Take a rotary phone apart in 3D, dial it, ring it, and hear why calls sound so "telephone-y".

→ A classic phone is a handset, a hook switch, a dial, two bells and two copper wires.
→ Lift the handset, the hook switch closes, and current flows from the exchange.
→ Your voice squeezes carbon granules, and the current in the wire copies the sound.
→ A rotary dial counts out your number by breaking the current: 7 breaks for a 7.
→ Touch-tone keys send two notes at once: 5 is 770 hertz plus 1,336 hertz.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/telephoneclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a telephone work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Your voice squeezes a pinch of carbon, a current copies the sound, and a switch that steps once per pulse finds the other phone. Take a rotary phone apart in 3D, dial it, ring it, and hear why calls sound so "telephone-y".

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/telephoneclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/telephoneclear

In this video:
• Two wires and a battery. A classic phone hangs on a pair of copper wires that run to the exchange.
• A voice becomes a current. In the mouthpiece, sound squeezes carbon granules behind a diaphragm.
• Dialling is counting. A rotary dial breaks the current once per step as it spins back, 10 times a second: 7 breaks for a 7, 10 for a 0.
• The exchange joins the wires. First operators plugged cords into jacks.
• Many calls share one line. Long-distance trunks carry voices as numbers: 8,000 samples a second, 8 bits each, 64 kbit/s per call.
• Why calls sound telephone-y. A classic phone channel carries only 300 to 3,400 Hz, enough for words but not for the deep boom or the hiss of a voice.
